Acid-base theories 
Acids and bases have opposing properties, and they neutralize each other 
when mixed together. The concepts of acidity and basicity can be extended to 
all classes of chemical compounds, including salts and oxides. 
According to the Arrhenius theory, acids produce protons (H* ions) and 
bases produce hydroxide ions (OH™) in aqueous solutions. The more general 
Brensted-Lowry theory defines acids as proton donors and bases as praoton 
acceptors. For example, aqueous hydrogen chloride is both an Arrhenius acid 
and a Brgnsted-Lowry acid: 
HCl(aq) — H'(aq) + Cl (aq) 
Gaseous ammonia is a Brensted-Lowry base but not an Arrhenius base, as 
it can accept protons (for example, from hydrogen chloride) but does not 
contain oxygen and thus cannot produce hydroxide ions: 
NH,(g) + HCl(g) — NH,CI(s) 
When an acid loses a proton, it forms its conjugate base, whereas a base forms 
its conjugate acid by accepting a proton. 
The ionization of hydrogen cyanide in water proceeds as follows: 
HCN(aq) + H,O(1) = H,0*(aq) + CN"(aq) 
a) ldentify the Brensted—-Lowry acids and Brensted—Lowry bases in this 
equilibrium. 
b) Identify two conjugate acid-base pairs in this equilibrium. 
Solution 
a) Brensted-Lowry acids: HCN(aq) and H,0*(aq). 
Brensted-Lowry bases: CN~(aq) and H,O(D). 
b) HCN(aq)/CN-(aq) and H,0*(aq)/H,0(1). 
Amphiprotic species, such as water, can both donate and accept protons: 
H,0(l) = H*(aq) + OH(aq) 
H,0() + H*(aq) = H,0%(aq) 
Amphoteric species can react with both acids and bases. All amphiprotic 
species are amphoteric, but not all amphoteric species are amphiprotic. For 
example, zinc oxide can react with both acids and bases, so it is amphoteric: 
ZnO(s) + 2H*(aq) — Zn*(aq) + H,0(1) 
ZnO(s) + 20H (aq) + H,0(1) — [Zn(OH),*(aq) 
At the same time, ZnQ cannot donate a proton (as it has none), so itis not 
amphiprotic.

Strong and weak acids and bases 
Strong acids, such as hydrogen chloride, HCI, dissociate completely in 
aqueous solutions while weak acids, such as ethanoic acid, CH,COOH, 
dissociate reversibly: 
HCl(aq) = H*(aq) + Cl(aq) 
CH,COOH(aq) = H*(aq) + CH,COO(aq) 
In addition to HCl, strong acids include sulfuric acid, H,SO,, nitric acid, HNO,, 
perchloric acid, HC104, chloric acid, HClOa, hydrogen bromide, HBr, and 
hydrogen iodide, HI. Almost all other acids are weak. 
Strong bases include all hydroxides of group 1 metals (Li to Cs) and some 
hydroxides of group 2 metals (Ca to Ba). All other bases are weak. 
NaOH(aq) — Na*(aq) + OH(aq) 
NH_(aq) + H,0(l) = NH,*(aq) + OH(aq)

Another common error is the

Assessment tip 
Strong acids and bases dissociate 
irreversibly, which is shown by the 
straight arrow (—) in equations. 
The dissociation schemes of weak 
acids and bases must include the 
equilibrium sign (=). 
The driving force of acid-base 
reactions is the formation of weak 
conjugates. The dissociation of 
the weak ethanoic acid is an 
unfavourable process, so only a 
small proportion of the acid exists 
as ions while most CH,COOH(aq) 
molecules remain undissociated. 
In contrast, the dissociation of the 
strong hydrochloric acid is 
irreversible because its conjugate 
base, Cl-(aq), is very weak and 
thus cannot gain a proton from 
water to form HCl(aq).

Titration and pH curves 
In a typical titration experiment, a solution of an acid or base of an unknown 
concentration is gradually neutralized by a standard solution of a base or acid 
that is added dropwise. 
The progress of the neutralization can be represented by a titration curve, 
which shows the pH of the reaction mixture as a function of the added volume 
of the standard solution. 
Example 6

b) Describe how the shape of the pH curve will differ if the solution of 
HCl(aqg) from part (a) is added to the solution of NaOH(aq) of the same

Solution 
a) Atthe beginning of the titration, the solution contains only 
HCl(aq), so the curve begins at pH = -log(0.10) = 1.00. Initially, the 
curve is almost horizontal. Approaching the equivalence point at 
V(NaOH) = 10.0cm?, the pH rises sharply to 7.0, where the mixture 
contains only NaCl(aq). Immediately after the equivalence point, the 
curve continues to rise sharply. When a large excess of the titrant has 
been added, the curve flattens out and gradually approaches the pH 
of the standard NaOH(aq) solution, 14 + 10g(0.10) = 13.00 (figure 1).

Buffer solutions 
Acid-base buffers contain conjugate weak acid—base pairs and resist changes 
in pH upon addition of small amounts of strong acids and bases. 
For example, an ethanoate buffer consists of a weak ethanoic acid and its 
conjugate base, ethanoate anion. When a small amount of astrong acid is 
added to this buffer, the strong acid is neutralized by the weak conjugate base 
of the buffer system, producing the weak conjugate acid: 
CH,COO(aq) + H*(aq) — CH,COOH(aq)

Similarly, a small amount of a strong base is neutralized by the weak conjugate 
acid of the buffer, producing the weak conjugate base: 
CH,COOH(aq) + OH-(aq) — CH,COO~(aq) + H,0(I) 
In both cases, the overall composition of the buffer solution (a conjugate 
acid-base pair) and thus its pH remain almost unchanged. 
Buffer solutions can be prepared by partial neutralization of weak acids or 
bases, or by mixing weak acids or bases with their salts. Common types of 
acid-base buffers are listed in table 5.
